— here are a few ideas 


TRY THIS WHEN LUNCH IS LATE! 

In the event it becomes necessary to 
kill ten or so minutes, why not have a 
zodiac lunch? 

Have a prepared f camper* horiscope for 
each zodiac sign. When the time comes 
to delay the group, suggest that each 
camper sit at his/her zodiac table and 
read the horiscope of each sign. 

Great fun - mixes the group and uses 
up the ten minutes.

Tree Silhouettes - Cut from black paper- 
outlines of: 

spruce, pine, elm, red cedar, weeping 
willow, sugar maple, poplar. 

Game of Touch - Players blindfolded- 
Natural objects placed in hands to 
identify: 

seeds, leaves, fruit, flowers, nuts, 
shells, feathers, vegetables, soils. 

Game of Smell - "Best smells" - blind¬ 
folded. Objects with distinct odours: 
mint, evergreen, wintergreen, balsam, 
skunk cabbage, onion, parsnip, turnip, 
cedar, apple, orange, mould, cucumber. 

Game of Taste - as above.

C.C. A. President... 


By the time you read this article, it 
will be winter and hopefully there will 
be ample snow for the skiers and lots of 
ice for the skaters. Winter camping 
will be in full swing, and those not 
involved in this activity will be busy 
with maintenance and preparations for 
another summer. 

The C.C.A. Leadership Resources Work¬ 
shop was held October 16-18 at Camp 
Wanakita in the Haliburton region of 
Ontario and was hosted by our genial 
Treasurer, Wayne Perkins. A great camp 
in a lovely setting. A Board Meeting 
followed the Workshop and we had good 
attendance with representation from 
every province. Everyone participated 
in the discussions and we owe a vote of 
sincere thanks to these dedicated cam¬ 
ping enthusiasts who give so generously 
of their time and expertise to help CCA. 
The work of the association continues to 
; grow and this speaks well of the indi¬ 
vidual efforts put forth. 

Jan James and Lou Lanier, two experien¬ 
ced and eager members from Alberta, 
were the faciltitators for the workshop. 
They did an excellent job in keeping 
thirty "individuals" on track. New 
ideas were put forth and many other on¬ 
going programs re-affirmed. Many of the 
delegates were new to C.C.A. and adapted 
well to this new responsibility. We wel¬ 
come them to the Board. Thank you - Lou 
and Jan, for the excellent job you did 
in organizing and carrying out this im¬ 
portant work. Marjorie Booth, Executive 
Director, was always available, lending 
a helping hand wherever needed. The 
main idea of the work shop was to de- 
I velop a three to five year plan for the 
C.C.A., and I believe we succeeded. The 
findings were then presented to the 
Board, a committee was formed to study 
the recommendations and prepare a report 
for consideration by the Board at its 
next meeting. 

You are all aware that the membership 
approved certain changes in our consti¬ 
tution and that we now have three re¬ 


gional vice-presidents. The paper work 
aspect of these changes took place du¬ 
ring the summer and early fall and the 
results were announced at the Board mee¬ 
ting. Derek Walsh of Montreal has agreed 
to stay on as the representative of Que¬ 
bec and Ontario until May, 1981. George 
Matthews, the most valued President of 
the N.S.C.A. was elected to represent the 
Atlantic Provinces until May, 1983. The 
Western Provinces did not have any nomi¬ 
nations submitted in time for election, 
so, upon their recommendation, Gary Luthy 
of Alberta has been appointed as the Wes¬ 
tern Regional Vice-President until May, 
1981. Welcome to all. We now hope that 
a lot of two way communication between 
C.C.A. and the provincial groups will 
take place through the medium of these 
gentlemen. 

John Latimer reports a busy summer of 
communication and meetings with the 
American Camping Association concerning 
the proposed 1983 International Congress. 
Finances proved to be too big an obsta¬ 
cle so that regretfully the joint effort 
of C.C.A./O.C.A. and A.C.A. has been 
dropped. However, C.C.A. and O.C.A. 
have agreed to jointly sponsor the In¬ 
ternational Congress in Toronto in March 
of *83. We hope that there will be ac¬ 
tive participation by our neighbors to 
the south and of course invite campers 
from other countries around the globe. 
John and his committee will soon be gi¬ 
ving us more details of the revised pLans. 

No doubt you have been receiving notice 
of the new publications available through 
the C.C.A. This is a growing and vital 
part of our work. Use this service when¬ 
ever possible and let the office know of 
other books that will be of interest to 
camping people. We wish to expend this 
service to our members and it is also a 
good source of revenue. 

Cliff Labbett

The COUNSELLOR'S Page 


This idea came from Camp Howdy in British Columbia and appeared in 
the October/November 1980, B.C.C.A. Newsletter. 

Camper Care Package 

At the Y.M.C.A.’s Camp Howdy near Vancouver, B.C., we have developed 
what we call a "Camper Care Package". Naturally it is modelled after 

the traditional Care Package concept that parents' use.. but with 

a difference. 

On the last day of camp each counsellor is responsible for packing a 
C.C.P. (Camper Care Package) in each of her or his campers' luggage, 
and requesting that it is not opened until the camper has reached 
home. Like a Care Package from home, campers look forward to opening 
their C.C.P. once they are home. Parents have given us excellent feed¬ 
back about our C.C.P.'s. 

Included in each C.C.P.are: (A new C.C.P. is made up every year 

so that returning campers have some¬ 
thing new to look forward to in the 
C.C.P.) 

1. A "What is a C.C.P." letter - written and signed by our camp mascot 

2. The words for some of the more popular camp songs, announcements, 
graces, etc. 

3. A special poem about camp, camp life, the out-of-doors or nature, 

4. Fun activities to do at home, such as crafts, games, etc., which 
are made up according to what age group the children fall into - 
either 7-8, 9 - 11 or 12 - 14. 

5. A meaningful (value-oriented) story made up according to the above 
age groupings. 

6. A list of special January to June Camp and local Y.M.C.A. programs 
each camper could become involved in and the addresses of their 
local Y.M.C.A. 

7. An evaluation form for parent(s) and child to complete together 
and return to our camp office. This also served the dual purpose 
of providing parents with additional ways of finding out more 
about their child's stay at camp. 

8. A family fun activity aimed at family interaction. 

If you wish any further information, contact Bruce Cox at the Y.M.C.A. Canping and 
Outdoor Recreation Branch, Y.M.C.A. of Greater Vancouver, 2556 Highbury Street, 
Vancouver, B.C., V6R 3T3.

THE C.C.A. 


L’A.C.C. 


The C.C.A. was founded in 1936 as anon- 
profit organization. It is a national 
federation of provincial camping asso¬ 
ciations uniting the camping leaders 
into an organization involved in the 
growth, development and promotion of 
camping in Canada. 

All Canadian Camping Association pro¬ 
grams and projects are made possible by 
membership fees, private contributions 
and funds from Fitness and Amateur 
Sport, Government of Canada. 

The Canadian Camping Association oper¬ 
ates a bookstore, primarily as a ser¬ 
vice to its members. Books of interest 
to camp directors, administrators, par¬ 
ents, counsellors and leaders working 
with children and youth in the outdoors 
are available in the Toronto office or 
may be ordered by mail or telephone. 

The books handled by C.C.A. are classi¬ 
fied into broad categories and listed 
alphabetically along with a brief de¬ 
scription of their contents, the pub¬ 
lisher and the price. There is an al¬ 
phabetical index and order forms at the 
end of this catalogue. 


L’Association canadienne des camps, creee 
en 1936, est un organisme a but non lucratif 
et une federation nationale des associations 
provinciales de camping reunissant les orga- 
nismes qui se vouent a la croissance et a 
1'expansion du camping au Canada. 

Tous les projets et programmes de 1’Association 
canadienne des camps sont realises grace aux 
cotisations des membres, aux contributions des 
particuliers et aux subventions de la Direction 
generale de la Condition physique et du Sport 
amateur du gouvernement federal. 

L’Association canadienne des camps offre un 
service de librairie a ses membres. Les livres 
interessant les responsables de camps d'enfants 
et d'adolescents (directeurs, administrateurs, 
parents, conseillers et moniteurs) sont dispo- 
nibles au siege social a Toronto. On accepte 
les commandes telephoniques ou postales. 

Nos publications sont divisees en categories 
generales. La liste alphabetique contient un 
resume succinct de chaque publication et indi- 
que l’editeur et le prix. A la fin du catalo¬ 
gue se trouvent la liste alphabetique des 
livres et des bons de commande. 


As well as selling books from both Ca¬ 
nadian and American sources, the C.C.A. 
publishes a number of titles and is the 
sole distributor in Canada for books 
published by the American Camping Asso¬ 
ciation. 


L’A.C.C. vend des livres canadiens et americains, 
ainsi que ses propres publications. De plus, 
elle est le seul distributeur des livres publies 
par 1'American Camping Association. 

Conditions 


Terms 

All prices are subject to change with¬ 
out notice. 

Unless payment accompanies your order 
shipping and handling charges will be 
added to the invoice. Third Class 
rates will be used unless faster ser¬ 
vice is requested. 


Tous les prix peuvent etre modifie sans preavis. 

Les frais de poste sont ajoutes au montant 
facture, a moins que le paiement ne soit 
effectue avec la commande. Generalement, les 
livres sont expedies par courrier de troisieme 
classe, mais il est possible, sur demande, 
d’adopter un service plus rapide. 


A service charge of 1% per month on the 
unpaid balance will be added to over¬ 
due accounts. 

We do not accept returns except in the 
case of error or damage. Authorization 
for such returns must be requested in 
advance. 

This publication is financially suppor¬ 
ted by the contributions program of 


Une surcharge de 1% par mois sera ajoute aux 
comptes en souffrance. 

Nous n'accepterons pas de livres en retour sauf 
en cas d’erreur ou de dommage. II faut en 
obtenir 1'autorisation a l'avance. 

La publication de cette brochure est financee 
par le programme de subventions du

PROJECT REACH 

These materials developed by Project Reach deal especially with the expan¬ 
sion and development of camping with the handicapped, although they are 
applicable to every camp in many ways. They are available to the Canadian 
Camping Association from the American Camping Association. Project Reach 
is funded by the U.S. Department of Health, Education and Welfare and is 
located at the University of Kentucky at Lexington. Four categories are planned. 

Camp Director Series .... not yet available 

Camp Managment Series 

Camp Staff Manual - 75p, 8§ X 11, three hole punched. Project Reach, 1979 7.50 

Good resource for a director writing a manual forhis camp. 

Camp Counsellor and Program Specialist Training Series 

Module One - An Orientation to Camping and the Camp , 68p. 8g X 11, 3 H.P., 7.00 


Module Two - Knowing the Campers , 80p, " " 7.50 
Module Three - Camp Program Planning and Leadership , 88p, " " 7.50 
Module Four - Camp Health and Safety Practices , 108p " " 5.50 
Module Five - Dealing with Camper Behavior , 116p, " " 7.50 
Module Six - Evaluating the Camp Experience , 128p, " " 8.00 


"Modules Two and Four deal more heavily with the handicapped camper; 
the other modules deal with generic skills common to staff working 
with any camper clientele." 

Camp Staff Series

General information as well a specifics on job as food supervisor.

162 games for adults or teenagers. 

(The) Handbook of Recreational Games - N. Boyd, 128p, Dover, 1975. 2.75 

18 categories of games with up to 59 (plus variations) in a category. 

Rules for common and uncommon games 

(The) New Games Book - A. Fluegelman, ed.l93p. Doubleday, 1977. 8.75 

"Play fair, play hard, nobody hurt." A collection of old and new games. 

Winning Through Cooperation - T. Orlick, 278p, Hawkins and Associates, 1978. 10.50 
Dr. Orlick offers exciting alternatives to such well knwon games as 
football, baseball, volleyball and soccer while revealing why the cur¬ 
rent emphasis on competition is so harmful. 

TRIPPING 

Guide to Canoe Camping - B. Johnstone, 64p, ACA, 1980. 4.95 

Information on planning, suggested trips, paddling and strokes, food and 
camping supplies, etc. An excellent manual for a leader planning a trip. 

* Path of the Paddle - B. Mason, 160p. hardcover. Van Nostrand Reinhold, 1980. 24.95 

Special price of 19.95 until December 31, 1980 A comprehensive and 
lavishly illustrated intructional guide for both the novice and expert. 

Wilderness Canoeing - J. Malo, 176p, Collier-MacMillan, 1971 6.50 

Information on where to find the shrinking wilderness and how to travel 
through by canoe. 

WATERFRONT 

Basic River Canoeing - R. McNair, 104p, ACA, 1969. 3.25 

Complete manual of white water canoeing. 

(A) Small Boat Sailor’s Bible - H. Smith, 147p, Collier-MacMillan, 1964 3.75 

Complete guide to buying, maintaining, and sailing small sailboats. 

Swimming - F. Waterman, 142p, Teach Yourself Books, 1970. 1.95 

Anyone who really practices the methods described here will improve ability. 

* Windsurfing - M. Gadd, J. Boothroyd, A. Durrell, 128p, Van Nostrand Reinhold, 9.95 

A Guide to Freesailing Techniques. 1980. 

WINTER CAMPING 

* (The) Concise Book of Winter Camping - T. Brown and R. Hunter, 63p, Gage,1978.2.95 

This illustrated book explains how too augment summer gear to winter stan¬ 
dards, what to buy, how to cope with cold, wind and snow and be comfortable. 

* Cross Country Canada - M. Keating, 212p, Van Nostrand Reinhold, 1977. 6.95 

Handbook and Trail Guide for Cross-Country Skiers. 

* Cross Country Ontario - M. Keating, 109p, Van Nostrand Reinhold, 1979. 3,95 

The only Ontario handbook and trail guide for X-Country Skiers - 275 listings 

Snow Sculpture and Ice Carving - J. Haskins, 91p, Collier-MacMillan, 1974 6.75 

How to pack snow together until you have: a cat, a duck family, monsters. 

How to chip away at ice until you have: a sailboat, fruitbasket, whales, etc. 



WOODSMANSHIP 


(The) Campcraft Book - C. Hammett, ACA, 1980. (price to be determined) 

A revised and updated version of Your Own Book of Campcraft . first pub¬ 
lished in 1950. A handy, authoritative book on campcraft skills. 

* (The) Complete Woodsman - P. Provencher, 225p, Habitex Book, 1974. 4.95 

A handbook for the serious woodsman, a basic guide to survival in the 
woods. Complete directions for every conceivable situation are included. 

Home in Your Pack - B. Angier, 202p, Collier-MacMillan, revised 1972. 2.75 

How to—do—it imanual details places to go, kinds of packs and equipment, 
clothes to wear and pack, and trail recipes. 

How to Stay Alive in the Woods - B. Angier, 286p, Collier-MacMillan, 1956. 2.75 

In its 14th printing - A complete guide to food, shelter and self-preser¬ 
vation. Originally published as Living Off the Country . 

(The) New Way of the Wilderness - C. Rutstrum, 280p, Collier-MacMillan,1958 3.95 
"A professional woodsmans methods of exploring, camping & surviving. 

Woodcraft and Camping - "Nessmuk" lOlp, Dover, 1963. 2.75 

The original woodcraft book - a classic through 3 or 4 generations. 

* Woodsmanship Leaders ’ Guide - K. Wipper, 155p, CCA, 1979. 6.00 

An exploration of the land ethic; a compendium of ideas on the theme of 
leadership, and a set of materials on land pursuits. An outgrowth of the 
C.C.A. National Woodsmanship Leaders’ Schools.

n-depth study of topics designed to help meet the challenges of the ' 80 's 


Facility Maintenance 

(11 hours) 

Wed. Feb. 25, 1:00-5:00 P.M. 

Thurs. Feb. 26, 9:00-12 noon 
1:00-5:00 P.M. 


John J. Murray, ASLA 
Program Specialist 
Girl Scouts of the USA 


Health Management 

(7 hours) 

Thurs. Feb. 26, 9:00-12 noon 
1:00-5:00 P.M. 


Dr. Luther B. Travis 
Professor 

Department of Pediatrics 
University of Texas Medical 
Branch, Galveston 


The author of the new and comprehensive Facility 
Maintenance Systems manual will present an eleven 
hour work session involving an in-depth study of this 
most important and crucial aspect of camp manage¬ 
ment. Mr. Murray will be joined by a panel of other 
experienced professionals in this field. The thorough¬ 
ness of their presentations will benefit the new as well 
as the experienced camp director. 


Food Management Dr. James C. Taylor 

(7 hours) Dean, Conrad Hilton College of 

Thurs. Feb. 26, 9:00-12 noon Hotel & Restaurant Management 
1:00-5:00 P.M. University of Houston 

Dr. Taylor and other distinguished faculty members of 
the Hilton College will expand our view and under¬ 
standing of professional food service operations. 

Interacting with these experienced educational lead¬ 
ers will indeed be a rare opportunity. 


Dr. Travis has been a camp Medical Director for more 
than 20 years. He has selected a well qualified team of 
doctors, nurses, and medical professionals to discuss 
issues, trends and acceptable health care practices. 


Business Management Robert L. Murphy, CPCU, CLU, l 
(5V2 hours) LLD 

Sat. Feb. 28, 10:30-1 2 noon Ehrman, Murphy & Company 
1:00-5:00 P.M. Houston, Texas 

Bob Murphy is past president of the Casualty Under¬ 
writers of Texas. For 25 years he has been involved 
with Risk Management for many Texas camps. Joining 
Mr. Murphy will be a team of attorneys, CPAs, and other 
professionals who will address current business trends 
and practices and their application to better camp 
management.

Only God Can Make A Tree 


This notice has been posted in the forest reserves of Portugal for 
over one thousand years. 

(Ecologists please note: "Everything old is new again.") 

"I am the heart of your hearth on the cold winter 
nights; the friendly shade which screens you from 
the summer sun; and my fruits quench your thirst 
as you journey on. 

I am the beam which supports your house, the board 
of your table, the bed on which you sleep and the 
timber which builds your boat. 

I am the handle of your hoe, the door of your home, 
the wood of your craddle and the shell of your cof¬ 
fin. 

I am the bread of kindness and the flower of beauty. 

You who pass by, please... listen to my prayer - 
’HARM ME NOT.

Thought for Food 


SKILLET PUDDING 

1 can (1 and 2/3 cups evaporated 
milk 

3/4 cup cocoa 
% cup sugar 
3/4 cup water 

Graham crackers, cookies etc. 

Put the first four ingredients in a 
skillet and bring them to a boil 
stiriring constantly. Add lo or so 
coarsely broken graham crackers and 
cook over low heat for about ^ hour. 

If graham crackers are not handy, 
other kinds of cookies can be used, 
or breakfast foods such as corn flakes 
even if they are a bit soggy! This is 
an easy tasty dessert, and is a good 
way to use up items that might other¬ 
wise be thrown away. Serves 6. 


ENERGY BARS 


Combine in a skillet over moderate 
heat about 2 cups of any one of a 
combination of ready-to-eat cereals 
e.g. "Grapenuts" and ’’Bran Flakes"; 
plus some raisins, nuts or coconut. 

The heating will crisp these ingredi¬ 
ents. Remove from heat and stir in, 
until melted, about 1 cup (6 oz pkg) 
of pieces of semi-sweet chocolate, 
drop by spoonfuls onto waxed paper or 
foil and let stand until firm. (The 
mixture will be very thick and hard to 
stir.) For use on trips, pat the mix¬ 
ture solidly into a muffin tin and turn 
out the cakes when they have cooled. 
Wrap in aluminum foil. If possible, 
make them in a double boiler, rather 
than a skillet. Makes 16. 


From Cookery for Kids, Kamp n* Kicks by Helen E. Stewart
